title_topic: Acute kidney injury and timing of renal replacement therapy
summary: A consultant-level review of renal replacement therapy (RRT) in ICU acute kidney injury. On timing: ELAIN (JAMA 2016, single centre, 231 patients) found lower 90-day mortality with early RRT. AKIKI (NEJM 2016, 620 patients), IDEAL-ICU (NEJM 2018, 488 patients with septic shock, stopped for futility) and STARRT-AKI (NEJM 2020, 3,019 randomised) found no mortality benefit. STARRT-AKI also found more adverse events with accelerated RRT and more RRT dependence at 90 days (10.4% vs 6.0%, RR 1.74). A 2025 post hoc analysis suggests this excess dependence comes mostly from starting RRT at all rather than starting it early. In the 2020 Lancet IPD meta-analysis, 28-day mortality was 44% vs 43%. Between about 38% and 49% of patients in the delayed arms never needed RRT. AKIKI2 (Lancet 2021) found no extra benefit from waiting beyond 72 hours of oliguria or a BUN of 112 mg/dL, and an adjusted secondary analysis showed a mortality signal (HR 1.65). BICARICU-2 (JAMA 2025) did not change mortality, though RRT use was lower with bicarbonate (a secondary outcome). On modality: Hemodiafe found no survival difference, and the excess dialysis dependence seen with intermittent RRT is an observational finding only. On dose: ATN and RENAL support delivering 20-25 mL/kg/h; LIMIT (12 vs 25 mL/kg/h) is ongoing. On anticoagulation: in RICH, citrate gave longer filter life and less bleeding than heparin, with no significant mortality difference and more new infections. On stopping: urine output without diuretics is the best predictor of success. LIBERATE-D (JAMA 2026, 221 stable patients on intermittent haemodialysis) found more recovery with a conservative dialysis strategy, but only in the unadjusted analysis. Long term, about 5% of RENAL day-90 survivors needed maintenance dialysis at four years, and albuminuria was common. On guidance: KDIGO 2012 is still current, and its 2026 AKI/AKD update completed public review in May 2026 and is awaiting publication. NICE NG148 (2019, updated 2024) and the 2020 joint Renal Association/BRS/ICS guideline both advise basing initiation on the whole patient.
takeaways: Without an emergent indication, early RRT does not reduce mortality, and waiting means roughly a third to a half of patients never need it.
Don't wait indefinitely: AKIKI2 gives a signal of harm from delaying beyond 72 hours of oliguria or a urea of about 40 mmol/L when nothing else has prompted RRT.
Deliver 20 to 25 mL/kg/h, and use regional citrate for CRRT unless there is a contraindication.
Choose modality on haemodynamic stability and brain injury, not dogma.
Watch urine output, don't use diuretics to speed weaning, and arrange kidney follow-up for survivors.
